title.narrative: Strengthening Civil Courage – Sahel

description.narrative: The Sahel has been the scene of large-scale armed conflict since 2012. Jihadist groups, state security forces, international military actors, and community militias and bandits are involved in these armed conflict. The conflict is exacerbated due to conflict between communities and weak state presence. There is economic underdevelopment, clientelism and corruption among elites. The programme in the Sahel will work with civil society actors to address these issues, common security and human rights problems.

The activity is part of a larger programme implemented by the Strengthening Civil Courage Alliance, consisting of ABAAD – Resource Center for Gender Equality, Amnesty International The Netherlands, DefendDefenders, PAX and their partner networks.

The main objective of the Sahel programme is for CSOs and human rights defenders, working in the tri-border region of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, to contribute to greater accountability and more inclusive conflict-sensitive policies through effective monitoring and documentation of human rights violations, advocacy, and inclusive dialogue for peace and justice. More specifically, the aim is for CSOs, female and young human rights defenders and activists to claim their civic space; that state actors increasingly respond to the pressure of citizens to build inclusive communities; and, for national governments and international military actors to adhere to international norms and human rights standards.

The main target groups are human rights defenders that work at national level on civic space, good governance and rule of law; human rights defenders involved in monitoring and reporting conflict-related human rights violations; civilian populations and communities in the Liptako Gourma border region; and, CSO partners from the three sides of the border.

title.narrative: Outcome 2.2 State actors acknowledge and investigate human rights violations, hold perpetrators to account and ensure adequate reparations for victims.
# (and description) of advocacy initiatives carried out by partner CSOs (networks and CSOs) towards new/adjusted/blocked laws, holding perpetrators to account, etc. (SCS4)

comment.narrative: All partners are well connected in civil society in their own countries, including in joint advocacy initiatives, and have a network of national informants. The partners are participating in consultation and advocacy platform with state and non-state actors.

PAX: One advocacy work was implemented by a partner to improve human rights' situation in prisons and in the areas affected by conflicts: a Law adopted by transitional assembly, revision of the Decree on prison's safeguards discipline; recruitment of interpretators;One advocacy work was done by another partner on the construction of cattle tracks to reduce land conflicts in Kaya and Boussouma. Both initiatives were implemented as planned with no major adjustments. The outcome of these advocacy initatives increased the respect for human rights in prisons for the first initiative and at the community level in relation to the second initiative. At the community level, this helped prevent inter-communal conflicts concerning the movements of livestock. We see no reason to change course in the project planning. However, we do foresee the need to review the implementation of the decree for prisons and the use of cattle tracks for resolving local conflicts.

Pax: One advocacy work was done by a PAX partner on taking into account the construction of livestock trails as well as their financing as a priority in the five-year development plan of the communes of Kaya and Boussouma
The context has changed to such an extent that it has become difficult to continue the MDR work in a manner which keeps to the principal of 'do no harm'.
While no advocacy initiatives were undertaken yet, all partner CSOs received capacity-building on lobby and advocacy to prepare for initiatives during the next year.

title.narrative: Programme reach
# of CSOs included in SPs (Strategic Partners) programmes

comment.narrative: Current partner portfolio comprises partner organisations with strong legitimacy at the community-level based on relevant track-records with significant public visibility of actions. All maintain good external relations that afford an important degree of access to authorities for L&A purposes, although activities with regard to the latter require strengthening for a number of partners. Partners were brought together with the aim of developing better coordination and synergy between different organizations and their separate initiatives. Alliance partners either share partner organisations and each strenghten different aspect of L&A advocacy (AINL MDR, PAX community dialogue and external relations, DD safety and security), or they invest in links between partners that are specialised in one of these fields.

DefendDefenders continued to strengthen and help built synergy within the National coalition of HRDs in Burkina Faso. Additionally, in 2023, a local ownership project was rolled out which seeks to engage all 10 partners in decision-making processes at the programme governance level. The pilot will be evaluated in 2024, but did help to build synergy among the Sahel partners. There is not yet a regional approach nor strategy on advocacy. There is a synergy to work on MDR, and a basis was laid in 2023 to add a ‘right to education focus’ to this MDR work. However, no actual fieldwork to monitor the right to education has taken place in 2023 in any of the concerned countries (as this will be rolled out in 2024). The partners are still in discussions with the rights to education consultant and should benefit from training on how to do monitoring before continuing the work. PAX is awaiting the preliminary conclusions / findings of the monitoring work to assess the follow-up to be given within the framework of regional advocacy. It is expected that more can be said on this topic in the reporting on 2024.

The ambition to create effective synergies between and strategies of partners will gradually be extended to the regional (cross-country) level over the course of the programme period. This is included in the learning question and will be documented at the end of the year. The pilot on local ownership will demonstrate if the platforms created for this pilot offer enough possibilities for exchange and joint strategizing.

DefendDefenders continued to work with the National coalition of HRDs in Burkina Faso on case assessment and verification.In addition, the local ownership pilot which started in May 2023 in the Sahel continued with a physical meeting in Ouagadougou in January 2024 and online meetings throughout the rest of the year. The Pilot was evaluated in June-July 2024 and the report is available. The pilot will continue until the end of the program. In 2024, the local ownership group (the advisory board) made strategic decisions on the focus on the right to education and the use of the gender funds made available by ABAAD and transferred to AINL.
The ambition to create effective synergies between and strategies of partners will gradually be extended to the regional (cross-country) level over the course of the programme period.

In 2022, the SCC programme organized a partners meeting in Ouagadougou with the objective of enlarging the alliance's footprint, knowledge and impact in the respective countries through deepening and strengthening the quality and results of the work within POV. In addition, the meeting aimed to develop the alliance’s integrated workplan for the first Semester and reflect on approaches and mechanisms to reinforce the alliance coordination, synergy and complementation. A local ownership pilot project will be implemented in 2023. This pilot project aims at improving ownership by partners in the SCC programme through testing ways to engage partners in the SCC programme in the Sahel in decision making on and management of the programme .

Joint learning sessions are foreseen to build bridges between the different partners and thus fulfill the ambition of creating effective synergies. In time this will also be pursued at the regional (cross-country) level.

Written agreements were concluded with seven partner organisations (see CSO partners list); in 2022, we aim to add two partners in Mali and one partner in Niger, so then the total should come to 10 partners.

By the end of 2025, 10 partners (2 women-led, 3 youth-led, 5 not youth or women-led) have actively engaged with alliance members in strategic decision-making. Please note that over the course of implementation, one partner changed from 'youth-led' to 'not youth-led or women-led'.

title.narrative: Outcome 3.1. Civil society in the Sahel have adequate lobby & advocacy capacities to meaningfully engage with international security actors (such as the EU)
# (and description of) advocacy actions carried out by CSOs regarding the role played by international security actors (SCS4)

comment.narrative: Since this is a new intervention, this baseline describes the situation in 2022. The role of CSOs as key stakeholders in consultation rounds for the development of international security policy by external actors such as the EU is underutilized.

3 partners, 2 from Burkina Faso and 1 from Niger, were brought to Brussels for an advocacy mission during the Belgian presidency of the EU council. The Belgian government prioritizes the Sahel as a key region in its foreign policy and advocates for continued EU engagement.

A regional roundtable mobilising 16 partners from Burkina Faso and Niger to discuss CSOs engagement with the EU. A basic insight document is available. This initiative represents a major readjustment of the programme because we initially planned to work on the topic of controversial weapons. However, due to the a change in the local context, specifically, the withdrawl of Barkhane, we decided to refocus our work on engaging EU representatives and local CSOs. In terms of the change process, we learned from this initiative that both local CSOs and EU representatives wish to meet and interact more often with regards to peace and stability in the Sahel. There are plans to follow-up on this initiative in 2023, specifically another roundtable and advocacy actions. These developments partain to MoFA indicator SCS4.
Advocacy actions carried out by CSOs follow a coherent and impactful strategy that succeeds in improving civil society engagement of international security actors

title.narrative: Outcome 2.1 Governments protect human rights in conflict areas, through new or reformed laws and regulations, including on armed self defence groups
# (and description) of laws, policies blocked, adopted, improved for inclusive peace and justice as a result of CSO engagement (SCS2)

comment.narrative: The persistence of armed violence in conflict areas across the Sahel is sustained by the absence (or harmful nature) of legal and policy frameworks. For example, the government of Burkina Faso passed legislation in January 2021 that enables local authorities to form groups of armed civilians to support state security forces. These have been responsible for civilian deaths and frequent abuses and thus risk exacerbating conflict dynamics.

A study was conducted on the unintended consequences of recent legislation enabling the arming of civilians. The study found worrying trends with regards to recruitment patterns, a shifting balance of power in favour of vigilantes, use of illegally procured firearms under the auspices of the government, and cases of abuse of civilians. The study will inform L&A initiatives to demand changes to existing legislation.

In 2022, (1) the Burkinabe government passed a Law that was adopted at the national assembly creating the presence of judicial police officers in all conflicts zones in order to strenghten the respect of human rights in the context of their fight against terrorism. (2) The Burkinabe government revised the law on VDPs (Volontaire de la Defense de Patrie) and included the obligation that recruited VDPs be trained in human rights and international humanitarian law. This was achieved thanks to the advocacy work carried out by PAX and its partners. These outcomes are important because both the governmental security forces and VDPs faced allegations of committing human rights violations and abuses under the framework of the fight against terrorism. VDPs were not initially trained in human rights awareness. Therefore, the revision of this law is a significant showing of respect for human rights in Burkina Faso. If well implemented, these laws will hold security forces and VDPs to account in the future.
Two new or reformed laws, regulations or government policies to protect human rights in conflict areas are adapted, in particular on the use of self-defense groups by national governments.

(2) The Burkinabe government revised the law on VDPs (Volontaire de la Defense de Patrie) and included the obligation that recruited VDPs be trained in human rights and international humanitarian law. This was achieved thanks to the advocacy work carried out by PAX and its partners. These outcomes are important because both the governmental security forces and VDPs faced allegations of committing human rights violations and abuses under the framework of the fight against terrorism. VDPs were not initially trained in human rights awareness. Therefore, the revision of this law is a significant showing of respect for human rights in Burkina Faso. If well implemented, these laws will hold security forces and VDPs to account in the future.

No law was adopted or revised in 2023. In fact the law was revised in 2022. In practice, at least 11 VDPs were dismissed in 2023 for “misconduct or for violating the texts in force”. The context did not allow advocacy work on human rights issues in Burkina Faso in 2023.

On December 26, 2024, Burkina Faso's Council of Ministers adopted a bill amending the Code of Criminal Procedure. PAX provided financial and technical support to the work of reviewing this code, which is awaiting adoption by the transitional assembly. This new code incorporates several new provisions for the protection of victims and witnesses, and reparation for victims, but will also help prevent prison overcrowding, which leads to human rights violations and radicalization in prisons. PAX continues monitoring the process of the adoption of this Bill by the transitional Assembly.
